newsitem.title: UK: Britain's budget -- possible tax changes and costs.
newsitem.headline: Britain's budget -- possible tax changes and costs.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke delivers his annual budget on Tuesday and will end weeks of speculation among politicians, financial markets and the man on the street.
A Reuter poll of 27 economists, conducted last week, found a consensus expecting tax cuts to the tune of 2.25 billion pounds ($3.8 billion), matched by planned cuts in government spending.
They would allow a one penny reduction in the basic rate of income tax but leave room for only tinkering elsewhere.
Following is a breakdown of possible tax changes Clarke may introduce and the costs or benefits to government finances that would result.

INCOME TAX - Most economists expect Clarke to take one penny off the basic rate of income tax, taking it to 23 percent. That would cost the government about two billion pounds. On top of that, an over-indexed increase in the personal allowance -- the part of an individual's income which is not taxed -- is forecast. The amount of income on which the 20 percent starting rate of income tax is paid also likely to be increased.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies said that at a cost of three billion pounds, the government could cut the basic rate of income tax to 22.5 pence, widen personal allowances by 450 pounds and widen the 20 percent starting band by 4,250 pounds.
Reducing the basic rate of income tax to 20 percent, the government's stated long-term aim, would cost a prohibitive 7.5 billion pounds, it said.

PROFIT-RELATED PAY - Profit-related pay links a portion of salaries to a company's performance, providing a theoretical incentive for boosting corporate profits. The part of the salary earmarked for PRP benefits from tax relief.

Members of parliament's Treasury Select Committee have said they expect Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to clamp down on tax relief on profit-related pay. But its complete abolition is unlikely, analysts say.
The IFS, which has proposed that PRP relief be phased out, estimates the present cost to the taxpayer at 1.5 billion stg in this financial year, compared with one billion in 1995/96.
INHERITANCE TAX
Prime Minister John Major has committed himself to abolishing inheritance tax in the future but it is unlikely to go in this budget, experts say. Any spare cash will be devoted to income tax cuts.
Inheritance tax is levied on an individual's estate after death or on assets transferred up to seven years before death.

At last year's budget, Clarke raised the exemption from inheritance tax to 200,000 stg from 154,000. That cost the government 130 million pounds. This year there is a reasonable chance of another increase in the exemption.

But a reduction in the rate at which inheritance tax is levied is not expected. The IFS said for each one percent point reduction from the present 40 percent rate, the government would lose about 15 million pounds.
CAPITAL GAINS TAX
The Conservatives have also pledged to get rid of capital gains tax in the future. The tax is levied on the real gains made on disposal of assets.
Last year the capital gains tax exemption was raised to 6,300 pounds from 6,000. A similar increase is possible this year but the IFS said it would only be tinkering.
Abolition would be very problematic without wholesale changes to the income tax system to prevent people from trying to convert income into assets to avoid tax.
Although relatively few people pay CGT, it raised 800 million pounds in revenue in 1994/95, the IFS said.

TAX CREDITS ON SHARE DIVIDENDS - Accountancy firm Coopers & Lybrand, in its survey of budget options, said that if the tax credit on equity dividend payouts is cut to 15 percent from 20 percent, it could save the Inland Revenue around 1.0 billion pounds a year, although this would take some time to come through. Clarke has already dabbled in this area. In October, he cancelled tax credits on share buyback schemes. That will yield about 400 million pounds, he said.
TAX ON TESSAS AND PERSONAL EQUITY PLANS - No changes expected by most pundits. ($1=.5941 Pound)
